Worship of images. See ''image-worship''.

'''worship''' (wėr′ship), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''worshiped'', ''worshipped'', ppr. ''worshiping'', ''worshipping''. [< ME. ''worshipen'', ''worshippen'', ''worschipen'', ''worschupen'', ''worshepen'', ''wurschepen'', ''worssipien'', ''wirchipen'', ''worthschipen'', ''wurthschipen'', ''wurthsupen'', ''worthsipien''; < ''worship'', ''n''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To honor; respect; regard with reverence, respect, or deference.
{{smaller block|<poem>He was a frynde to my fader, & a fyn louer,
''Worshippit'' hym on allwise & his will did.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 5278.}}
Therfore oughte Men to ''worshipe'' it and holde it more worthi than any of the othere. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 14.}}}}
'''2.''' To show respect to; treat with consideration or honor; pay one’s respects to.
{{smaller block|<poem>I grette the goode mon as the gode wyf me tauȝte,
And afterward his wyf, I ''worschupet'' hem bothe,
And tolde hire the tokenes that me i-tauȝt were.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), xi. 168.}}
Wee suffered to see the most noble queene of the world for to bee shamed openly, considering that her lord and our lord is the man of most worship in the world, and the most christned; and hee hath alway ''worshiped'' us all in all places. {{right|''Sir T. Malory'', Mort d’Arthure, III. cix.}}
<poem>To love one maiden only, cleave to her,
And ''worship'' her by years of noble deeds,
Until they won her.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Guinevere.}}}}
'''3.''' Specifically, to adore; pay divine honors to; show reverence to, with supreme respect and veneration; perform religious service to.
{{smaller block|<poem>He is fader of fei that formed ow alle
Bothe with fel and with face, and ȝaf ow fyue wittes,
Forte ''worschupen'' him therwith, while ȝe beoth heere.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), i. 15.}}}}

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|worry|6982|'''worship'''}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|<poem>And, like a fool, did eat the cow,
And ''worried'' on the tail.</poem>
{{right|''Marquis of Huntley’s Retreat'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 270).}}}}
{{smaller block|Ye have fasted lang and ''worried'' on a midge.
{{right|''Ramsay’s Scotch Proverbs'', p. 82. (''Jamieson.'')}}}}
'''2.''' To fight, as dogs, by seizing and biting at each other; be engaged in biting, shaking, or mangling with the teeth.—'''3.''' To be unduly anxious and careful; give way to anxiety; be over-solicitous or disquieted about things; borrow trouble; fret.
{{smaller block|Sensitive people, those who are easily wounded and discouraged, are most apt to ''worry'' when affairs go wrong, and yet they are just those whom worry will harm the most and who will lose the most in life by indulging in it.
{{right|''Alien. and Neurol.'', VIII. 141.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To worry along''', to get along by constant effort; keep on in spite of petty difficulties and anxieties. [Colloq.]}}
{{smaller block|By and by, if I can ''worry along'' into tolerable strength, . . . I am going off—say in mid-winter—to the south of England.
{{right|''S. Bowles'', in Merriam, II. 431.}}}}

'''worry''' (wur′i), ''n.''; pl. ''worries'' (-iz).   [< ''worry'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of worrying or biting and mangling with the teeth; the act of killing by biting and shaking.
{{smaller block|They will open on the scent . . . and join in the ''worry'' as savagely as the youngest hound.
{{right|''Lawrence'', Sword and Gown, iii.}}}}
'''2.''' Harassing anxiety, solicitude, or turmoil; perplexity arising from over-anxiety or petty annoyances and cares; trouble: as, it is not work but ''worry'' that kills; the ''worries'' of housekeeping.
{{smaller block|Among over-burdened people extra trouble and ''worry'' imply, here and there, break-downs in health, with their entailed direct and indirect sufferings.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Man vs. State, p. 51.}}}}

'''worrying''' (wur′i-ing), ''p. a.'' Teasing; troubling; harassing; fatiguing: as, a ''worrying'' day.
{{smaller block|<poem>Grave is the Master’s look; his forehead wears
Thick rows of wrinkles, prints of ''worrying'' cares.</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', The School Boy.}}}}

'''worryingly''' (wur′i-ing-li), ''adv.''   [< ''worrying'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a worrying manner; teasingly; harassingly.

'''worschipen†''', ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''worship.''

'''worse''' (wėrs), ''a. compar.''   [I. compar. ''worse''; early mod. E. also ''warse'', ''wars''; < ME. ''wors'', ''wurse'', ''wirse'', ''werse'', ''wors'', ''wers'', < AS. ''wirsa'', ''wyrsa'' = OS. ''wirsa'' = OFries. ''wirra'', ''werra'' = MHG. ''wirser'' = Icel. ''verri'' = Sw. ''värre'' = Dan. ''værre'' = Goth. ''wairsiza'', worse; with compar. suffix (lost or assimilated in the later forms, but appearing in the Goth. ''wairsiza''), prob. from a Teut. root appearing in OHG. ''werran'' (G. ''wirren''), twist, entangle, confuse (> OHG. ''werra'', confusion, broil, war), perhaps allied to L. ''verrere'' (pret. ''verri'', pp. ''versus''), whirl, toss about, drive, sweep along. Cf. ''war''<sup>1</sup>, and see ''war''<sup>2</sup> (Sc. ''waur'', etc.), ult. a doublet of ''worse''. Cf. ''worser''. II. superl. ''worst'', < ME. ''worste'', ''werste'', ''wurst'', < AS. ''wyrsta'', ''wyrsesta'', also by assimilation ''wyrresta'', = OS. ''wirsista'' = OHG. ''wirsisto'', ''wirsesto'', contr. ''wirst'' = Icel. ''verstr'' = Sw. ''värst'' = Dan. ''værst'', worst, superl. of the preceding. The ''s'' belongs to the root.]   '''1.''' The comparative of ''bad'', ''evil'', ''ill''; more bad, evil, ill, unfortunate, or undesirable; less valuable or perfect; more unfavorable or unsuccessful; less well in health, or less well off in worldly circumstances. See ''bad'', ''evil'', and ''ill.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Me think the ''wers'' part is mine;
to take the fleshe if I assay,
then the blode wil ryn a-way;
for-done ȝe haue me with ȝour dome.</poem>
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 111.}}}}
{{smaller block|Men . . . [who] unneth can speake one hole sentence in true latine, but, that ''wars'' is, hath all lernynge in derision.
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, i. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|She . . . was nothing bettered, but rather grew ''worse.''
{{right|Mark v. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What were thy lips the ''worse'' for one poor kiss?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 207.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Sir Oliver S.'' You have had no opportunity of showing your talents.

''Moses.'' None at all; I hadn’t the pleasure of knowing his distresses till he was some thousands ''worse'' than nothing.
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But what gave rise
To no little surprise,
Nobody seemed one penny the ''worse!''</poem>
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 212.}}}}
{{smaller block|Sometimes used substantively in the sense of something less good, desirable, fortunate, favorable, etc.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus bad begins and ''worse'' remains behind.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4. 179.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ah, farewell,
Lest of mine eyes thou shouldst have ''worse'' to tell
Than now thou hast.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 307.}}}} 2. In ''logic'', having, as a proposition, a character which, if belonging to one of two or more premises, must also belong to the conclusion. {{smaller|Thus, a negative is held to be worse than an affirmative proposition, and a particular worse than a universal. On the same principle, a spurious proposition is taken as in a second degree of particularity.—'''The worse''', the less desirable part or share; disadvantage; defeat; loss: hence, ''to put to the worse'', to defeat or discomfit; ''to have the worse'', to fare badly; come out of any contest or business worse than before.}}

<poem>The folk of Troie hemselven so misleden
That with ''the wors'' at nyght homward they fledden.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|Longe it endured that oon cowde not sey whiche party ''had the werse''.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 459.}}}}
{{smaller block|His enemyes preuailed and ''put'' his hoste ''to the worse'', he being sore wounded.
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, i. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|And Judah was ''put to the worse'' before Israel; and they fled every man to their tents.
{{right|2 Ki. xiv. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|I cannot tell who ''had the worse''.
{{right|''Playe of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 420).}}}}

'''worse''' (wėrs), ''adv. compar.''   [I. compar. ''worse'', < ME. ''wors'', ''wurs'', ''wers'', etc., < AS. ''wyrs'' = OS. ''wirs'' = MLG. ''wers'' = MHG. ''wirs'' = Icel. ''verr'' = Goth. ''wairs'', worse; with compar. suffix, lost in the adv. (as with ''bet''<sup>1</sup>): see ''worse'', ''a.'' II. superl. ''worst'', < ME. ''worst'', ''werst'', < AS. ''wyrst'' = Icel. ''verst'' = Sw. ''värst'' = Dan. ''værst'', worst, superl. of ''worse'': see above.]   '''1.''' In a more evil, wicked, severe, or disadvantageous manner; in a way that is less good, desirable, or favorable.

{{smaller block|We will deal ''worse'' with thee than with them.
{{right|Gen. xix. 9.}}}}
<poem>He is deformed, crooked, old, and sere,</poem>
{{smaller block|<poem>Ill-faced, ''worse'' bodied, shapeless everywhere.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iv. 2. 20.}}}}
{{smaller block|O Master Mayberry! before your servant to dance a Lancashire hornpipe! it shews ''worse'' to me than dancing does to a deaf man that sees not the fiddles.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' In a less or lower degree; less.
{{smaller block|Thou shalt serve me: if I like thee no ''worse'' after dinner, I will not part from thee. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4. 44.}}}}
'''3.''' Less favorably or agreeably.
{{smaller block|Then this they take ''worse'' than his working of miracles, or his working upon the Sabbath, That he would say that God was his Father. {{right|''Donne'', Sermons, xviii.}}}}
'''4.''' With more severity, intensity, etc.; in a greater degree.
{{smaller block|<poem>That honorable grief lodged here which burns
''Worse'' than tears drown.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 1. 112.}}}}

'''worse†''' (wėrs), ''v.''   [< ME. ''wersen'', ''wursen'', ''worsen'', < AS. ''wyrsian'', become worse, < ''wyrsa'', worse: see ''worse'', ''a.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To become worse.
{{smaller block|Werihede, thet maketh thane man weri and ''worsi'' uram daye to daye. {{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 33.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To worst; put to disadvantage; discomfit.
{{smaller block|<poem>Weapons more violent, when next we meet,
May serve to better us, and ''worse'' our foes.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 440.}}}}

'''worsen''' (wėr′sn), ''v.''   [= Icel. ''versna''; < ''worse'' + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''worse'', ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To grow worse; deteriorate. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|All the changing volitions of daily life, bettering or ''worsening'' as we advance in years.
{{right|''Maudsley'', Body and Will, p. 70.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make worse; cause to deteriorate.

{{smaller block|It is still Episcopacie that before all our eyes ''worsens'' and sluggs the most learned and seeming religious of our Ministers. {{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}
{{smaller block|The working-men are left to foolish devices, and keep ''worsening'' themselves; the best heads among them forsake their born comrades, and go in for a house with a high door-step and a brass knocker. {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, v.}}}}
'''2.''' To obtain advantage of.   ''Southey.'' [Rare.]

'''worser''' (wėr′sėr), ''a.'' and ''adv.''   [< ''worse'' + ''-er''<sup>3</sup>; a double compar. form (like ''lesser''), due to the fact that ''worse'' (like ''less'') is not obviously a compar. form.]   An old and redundant comparative of ''worse.''
{{smaller block|I cannot hate thee ''worser'' than I do.
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 5. 90.}}}}
{{smaller block|Fools! they their ''worser'' Thraldom still retain’d!
{{right|''Cowley'', Davideis, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou ’rt ''worser'' than a hog. {{right|''J. Baillie.''}}}}

'''worsett†''', ''n.'' and ''a.'' An old variant of ''worsted.''

'''worship''' (wėr′ship), ''n.''   [< ME. ''worship'', ''worshipe'', ''worshippe'', ''worshepe'', ''worschip'', ''wurship'', ''wurschipe'', ''wirschip'', ''wurthshipe'', ''worthschipe'', ''worthschepe'', ''worthssipe'', ''wurthschipe'', ''würthscipe'', < AS. ''weorthscipe'', ''wyrthscipe'', honor, < ''weorth'', ''wurth'', worthy, honorable, + ''-scipe'' (> E. ''-ship''): see ''worth''<sup>2</sup>, ''a.'', and ''-ship.'']   '''1.''' Honor; dignity; distinction; worthiness; honorable character or condition; good name; credit.
{{smaller block|<poem>Brynges wyues into wondur thaire ''worship'' to lose;
And ertes ay to euyll ende & ernyst by the last.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2942.}}}}

{{smaller block|That were to me grete ''wurship'', yef I sholde dye for my lorde.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 66.}}}}
{{smaller block|Upon paine of my life, this young knight shall come unto great ''worship''.
{{right|''Sir T. Malory'', Mort d’Arthure, III. xxxii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Keep smooth your face, and still maintain your ''worship''
With Berinthia.</poem>
{{right|''Shirley'', Maid’s Revenge, ii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' The outward recognition of merit; reverence; respect; deference.
{{smaller block|Then shalt thou have ''worship'' in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee.
{{right|Luke xiv. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|Knighthood is a Dignity, but Esquires and Gentlemen are but Names of ''Worship''.
{{right|''Guillim'', Display of Heraldry (1724), ii. 266.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Kings are like stars: they rise and set, they have
The ''worship'' of the world, but no repose.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Hellas.}}}}
'''3.''' Specifically, the reverence and homage which is or ought to be paid to God or a deity; adoration, sacrifice, praise, prayer, thanksgiving, or other devotional acts performed in honor of the Supreme Being or a god, and as part of religion.
{{smaller block|Nor are mankind simply content with this mock-''worship'' of God, but also impose and father it upon him, as if he had chose and ordained it.
{{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, ii., Expl.}}}}
{{smaller block|The allies, after conquering together, return thanks to God separately, each after his own form of ''worship''.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Gladstone on Church and State.}}}}
{{smaller block|The happiest man is he who learns from nature the lesson of ''worship''.
{{right|''Emerson'', Nature, p. 75.}}}}
'''4.''' Fervent esteem, admiration, or devotion; adoration.

{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis not your inky brows, your black silk hair,
Your bugle eyeballs, nor your cheek of cream,
That can entame my spirits to your ''worship''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 5. 48.}}}}
{{smaller block|Loyalty, Discipleship, all that was ever meant by Hero-''worship'', lives perennially in the human bosom.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Boswell’s Johnson.}}}}

'''5.''' Praise; glorification; celebration.
{{smaller block|And therfore thei don gret ''Worschipe'' thereto, and kepen it [an oak tree] full besyly. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 69.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I made hire to the ''worshipe'' of my lord: . . .
Thus semeth me that Nature wolde seye.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Physician’s Tale, l. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thai honurd the mount of caluary,
In ''wirschip'' of the cros namely.</poem>
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 90.}}}}

'''6.''' A title of honor used in addressing certain magistrates and others of rank or station. Abbreviated ''wp.''
{{smaller block|My father desires your ''worship’s'' company.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1. 271.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Dap.'' Is this the cunning-man?
''Face.'' This is his ''worship''.
''Dap.'' Is he a doctor?
''Face.'' Yes. ''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, i. 1.</poem>}}

'''House''' (or '''place''') '''of worship.''' (''a''†) A house or place of distinction.
{{smaller block|As sche hadde seyn hused [used] in ''places of worschip''.
{{right|''Paston Letters'', III. 314.}}}}
(''b'') A church or chapel; a place devoted to the worship of God.
{{smaller block|It is very probable that the Church of Kirkdale was considered in Doomsday-Book as the ''place of worship'' belonging to that manor. {{right|''Archæologia'', V. 197.}}}} Worship of images. See ''image-worship''.

''worshipen'', ''worshippen'', ''worschipen'', ''worschupen'', ''worshepen'', ''wurschepen'', ''worssipien'', ''wirchipen'', ''worthschipen'', ''wurthschipen'', ''wurthsupen'', ''worthsipien''; < ''worship'', ''n''.]   '''I.''' {{smaller block|Wee suffered to see the most noble queene of the world for to bee shamed openly, considering that her lord and our lord is the man of most worship in the world, and the most christned; and hee hath alway ''worshiped'' us all in all places. {{right|''Sir T. Malory'', Mort d’Arthure, III. cix.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To love one maiden only, cleave to her,
